## Background

Given an $n\times n$ nonsingular matrix $A$, its **inverse** $A^{-1}$ is the unique
matrix satisfying $A A^{-1} = A^{-1} A = I_n$.  Once $A^{-1}$ is known, each new
system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is answered by $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ at
$O(n^2)$ cost.  A stored LU factorization of $A$ gives the same $O(n^2)$ cost per
right-hand side (two triangular solves), takes about a third of the work to compute
(roughly $\tfrac{2}{3}n^3$ operations against $2n^3$ for $A^{-1}$), and in floating
point usually gives the more accurate solution.  So even with many right-hand sides,
LU is the better way to solve systems; the inverse is mainly useful in theoretical
analysis, or when its entries themselves are wanted (as with the Hilbert matrix
below).

## Theorem — Computing the Inverse by Gauss–Jordan

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Theorem — Inverse Matrix

Assume $A$ is an $n\times n$ nonsingular matrix.  Form the $n\times 2n$ augmented
matrix $[A\,|\,I_n]$.  Apply Gauss–Jordan elimination (reducing every column, not
just forward elimination) until the identity $I_n$ occupies the first $n$ columns.
Then $A^{-1}$ occupies columns $n+1$ through $2n$:

$$
[A \mid I_n] \xrightarrow{\text{Gauss–Jordan}} [I_n \mid A^{-1}].
$$
:::

The algorithm uses the same row operations as Gauss–Jordan elimination for solving
$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ but applies them simultaneously to $n$ right-hand sides
(the columns of $I_n$).

## Algorithm — Complete Gauss–Jordan Elimination

For $j = 1, 2, \ldots, n$ (pivot column):

1. Find the entry of largest absolute value in column $j$ at or below row $j$; swap
   that row with row $j$ (partial pivoting for numerical stability).
2. Divide row $j$ by the pivot $a_{jj}$ so that $a_{jj} = 1$.
3. For every other row $i \neq j$: subtract $a_{ij}$ times row $j$ from row $i$,
   zeroing the entire column $j$ above *and* below the pivot.

After all $n$ steps the left half of the augmented matrix is $I_n$ and the right
half is $A^{-1}$.

## Example 1 — Inverse of a $4\times 4$ Matrix

Find the inverse of

$$
A =
\begin{pmatrix}
4 & 8 & 4 &  0 \\
1 & 4 & 7 &  2 \\
1 & 5 & 4 & -3 \\
1 & 3 & 0 & -2
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

### Solution

Form the $4\times 8$ augmented matrix $[A \mid I_4]$:

$$
\left(
\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
4 & 8 &  4 &  0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & 4 &  7 &  2 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & 5 &  4 & -3 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
1 & 3 &  0 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}
\right).
$$

For hand computation we take the pivots in order without row interchanges and
postpone dividing by the pivots to the end.  The algorithm above would swap $R_2$
and $R_3$ at step 2 (pivot $3$) and normalize each pivot row as it goes, so its
intermediate matrices differ, but it reaches the same $A^{-1}$.

**Step 1 — Eliminate column 1** (pivot $= 4$; subtract multiples of $R_1$ from
$R_2, R_3, R_4$):

$$
\left(
\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
4 &  8 &  4 &  0 &  1    &  0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 &  2 &  6 &  2 & -\tfrac{1}{4} &  1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 &  3 &  3 & -3 & -\tfrac{1}{4} &  0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 &  1 & -1 & -2 & -\tfrac{1}{4} &  0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}
\right).
$$

**Step 2 — Eliminate column 2** (pivot $= 2$; also clear $R_1$):

$$
\left(
\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
4 &  0 & -20 & -8 &  2            & -4          & 0 & 0 \\
0 &  2 &   6 &  2 & -\tfrac{1}{4} &  1          & 0 & 0 \\
0 &  0 &  -6 & -6 &  \tfrac{1}{8} & -\tfrac{3}{2} & 1 & 0 \\
0 &  0 &  -4 & -3 & -\tfrac{1}{8} & -\tfrac{1}{2} & 0 & 1
\end{array}
\right).
$$

**Step 3 — Eliminate column 3** (pivot $= -6$; clear $R_1, R_2, R_4$):

$$
\left(
\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
4 & 0 &  0 & 12 &  \tfrac{19}{12} &  1            & -\tfrac{10}{3} & 0 \\
0 & 2 &  0 & -4 & -\tfrac{1}{8}   & -\tfrac{1}{2} &  1             & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -6 & -6 &  \tfrac{1}{8}   & -\tfrac{3}{2} &  1             & 0 \\
0 & 0 &  0 &  1 & -\tfrac{5}{24}  &  \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{2}{3}  & 1
\end{array}
\right).
$$

**Step 4 — Eliminate column 4** (pivot $= 1$; clear $R_1, R_2, R_3$), then
normalize $R_1, R_2, R_3$ by their diagonal entries:

$$
\left(
\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 &  \tfrac{49}{48} & -\tfrac{5}{4} &  \tfrac{7}{6} & -3 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & -\tfrac{23}{48} &  \tfrac{3}{4} & -\tfrac{5}{6} &  2 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 0 &  \tfrac{3}{16}  & -\tfrac{1}{4} &  \tfrac{1}{2} & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & -\tfrac{5}{24}  &  \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{2}{3} &  1
\end{array}
\right).
$$

The inverse is

$$
A^{-1} =
\begin{pmatrix}
 \tfrac{49}{48} & -\tfrac{5}{4} &  \tfrac{7}{6} & -3 \\[4pt]
-\tfrac{23}{48} &  \tfrac{3}{4} & -\tfrac{5}{6} &  2 \\[4pt]
 \tfrac{3}{16}  & -\tfrac{1}{4} &  \tfrac{1}{2} & -1 \\[4pt]
-\tfrac{5}{24}  &  \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{2}{3} &  1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Note: $\det(A) = -48$ (verified by cofactor expansion).

### Verification

Compute the first column of $A A^{-1}$ (it should equal $e_1 = (1,0,0,0)^T$):

| Row | $\sum_j A_{ij}(A^{-1})_{j1}$ | Result |
|-----|-------------------------------|--------|
| 1 | $4\cdot\tfrac{49}{48} + 8\cdot(-\tfrac{23}{48}) + 4\cdot\tfrac{3}{16} + 0$ | $\tfrac{196-184}{48}+\tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{12}{48}+\tfrac{36}{48} = 1$ $\checkmark$ |
| 2 | $\tfrac{49}{48} + 4\cdot(-\tfrac{23}{48}) + 7\cdot\tfrac{3}{16} + 2\cdot(-\tfrac{5}{24})$ | $\tfrac{49-92+63-20}{48} = 0$ $\checkmark$ |
| 3 | $\tfrac{49}{48} + 5\cdot(-\tfrac{23}{48}) + 4\cdot\tfrac{3}{16} + (-3)\cdot(-\tfrac{5}{24})$ | $\tfrac{49-115+36+30}{48} = 0$ $\checkmark$ |
| 4 | $\tfrac{49}{48} + 3\cdot(-\tfrac{23}{48}) + 0 + (-2)\cdot(-\tfrac{5}{24})$ | $\tfrac{49-69+20}{48} = 0$ $\checkmark$ |

## The Hilbert Matrix

Hilbert matrices appear naturally in polynomial approximation problems and are
classic examples of severely ill-conditioned matrices.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Definition — Hilbert Matrix

The **Hilbert matrix** $H_n$ of order $n$ has elements

$$
(H_n)_{ij} = \frac{1}{i+j-1}, \quad i,j = 1,\ldots,n.
$$
:::

The Hilbert matrices of orders 2, 3 and 4 are:

$$
H_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1 & \tfrac{1}{2}\\\tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix},
\quad
H_3 = \begin{pmatrix}1&\tfrac{1}{2}&\tfrac{1}{3}\\\tfrac{1}{2}&\tfrac{1}{3}&\tfrac{1}{4}\\\tfrac{1}{3}&\tfrac{1}{4}&\tfrac{1}{5}\end{pmatrix},
\quad
H_4 = \begin{pmatrix}
1&\tfrac{1}{2}&\tfrac{1}{3}&\tfrac{1}{4}\\
\tfrac{1}{2}&\tfrac{1}{3}&\tfrac{1}{4}&\tfrac{1}{5}\\
\tfrac{1}{3}&\tfrac{1}{4}&\tfrac{1}{5}&\tfrac{1}{6}\\
\tfrac{1}{4}&\tfrac{1}{5}&\tfrac{1}{6}&\tfrac{1}{7}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Ill-Conditioning of Hilbert Matrices

Hilbert matrices become extremely ill-conditioned as $n$ grows.  For $n=5$ the
2-norm condition number is $\kappa(H_5) \approx 4.77 \times 10^5$: a small relative
change in the data can change the inverse, or a solution, by up to about
$5\times10^5$ times as much (Example 2 below).  Inverting $H_5$ in double precision
(about 16 digits) still gives every entry to about 12 digits, but by $n=12$,
$\kappa(H_{12}) \approx 1.7\times10^{16}$ and a computed inverse typically has only
one or two correct digits: its relative error (2-norm) is usually between about 1%
and 20%, and it varies erratically with the method and with last-bit rounding of
the entries (about 6% to 9% for the correctly rounded $H_{12}$; occasionally much
smaller or larger).  The exact formulas below give
$H_n^{-1}$ with no rounding at all.
:::

## Inverse Hilbert Matrix

An exact closed-form formula for the inverse exists.  It can be expressed in two
equivalent ways.

**Factorial form:**

$$
(H_n^{-1})_{ij} = \frac{(-1)^{i+j}}{i+j-1}
  \cdot\frac{(n+i-1)!\,(n+j-1)!}{\bigl[(i-1)!\,(j-1)!\bigr]^2\,(n-i)!\,(n-j)!}.
\tag{7}
$$

**Binomial-coefficient form:**

$$
(H_n^{-1})_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}(i+j-1)
  \binom{n+i-1}{n-j}
  \binom{n+j-1}{n-i}
  \binom{i+j-2}{i-1}^{\!2}.
\tag{8}
$$

**Example:** for $n=5$ the formulas yield the exact integer matrix

$$
H_5^{-1} =
\begin{pmatrix}
     25 &    -300 &    1050 &   -1400 &    630 \\
   -300 &    4800 &  -18900 &   26880 & -12600 \\
   1050 &  -18900 &   79380 & -117600 &  56700 \\
  -1400 &   26880 & -117600 &  179200 & -88200 \\
    630 &  -12600 &   56700 &  -88200 &  44100
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

*Verification of entry $(1,1)$:* $(H_5^{-1})_{11} = (-1)^2 \cdot 1 \cdot \binom{5}{4}\binom{5}{4}\binom{0}{0}^2 = 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 1 = 25$ $\checkmark$

*Verification of entry $(1,2)$:* $(H_5^{-1})_{12} = (-1)^3 \cdot 2 \cdot \binom{5}{3}\binom{6}{4}\binom{1}{0}^2 = -2 \cdot 10 \cdot 15 \cdot 1 = -300$ $\checkmark$

## Example 2 — The Hilbert Matrix Rounded to Six Decimals

Round each entry of $H_5$ to six decimal places (Mathews calls this the chopped
Hilbert matrix) and find the inverse of

$$
A =
\begin{pmatrix}
1        & 0.5      & 0.333333 & 0.25     & 0.2 \\
0.5      & 0.333333 & 0.25     & 0.2      & 0.166667 \\
0.333333 & 0.25     & 0.2      & 0.166667 & 0.142857 \\
0.25     & 0.2      & 0.166667 & 0.142857 & 0.125 \\
0.2      & 0.166667 & 0.142857 & 0.125    & 0.111111
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

### Solution

Gauss–Jordan elimination on $[A \mid I_5]$, carried out in exact rational arithmetic
so that no further rounding enters, gives (to two decimals)

$$
A^{-1} \approx
\begin{pmatrix}
   26.93 &    -336.02 &    1205.11 &   -1634.03 &     744.41 \\
 -336.02 &    5471.18 &  -21788.96 &   31237.24 &  -14729.52 \\
 1205.11 &  -21788.96 &   91810.65 & -136343.92 &   65859.12 \\
-1634.03 &   31237.24 & -136343.92 &  207458.85 & -102006.85 \\
  744.41 &  -14729.52 &   65859.12 & -102006.85 &   50845.21
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

No entry of $A$ differs from the corresponding entry of $H_5$ by more than
$3.4\times10^{-7}$, yet $A^{-1}$ is far from the exact $H_5^{-1}$ above: entry
$(4,4)$ is $207458.85$ instead of $179200$, an error of $28258.85$ (16%), and entry
$(1,1)$ is $26.93$ instead of $25$.  Measured in the 2-norm, a relative change of
$3.9\times10^{-7}$ in the matrix has become a relative change of $0.16$ in its
inverse, a magnification of about $4\times10^5$, close to
$\kappa(H_5) \approx 4.77\times10^5$.

### Verification

In exact arithmetic $A A^{-1} = I_5$ (for example, row 1 of $A$ times the exact
$A^{-1}$ is $(1, 0, 0, 0, 0)$), so the matrix above is the true inverse of the
rounded matrix, to the two decimals shown.  The error is caused by rounding the data, not by the elimination:
a double-precision inversion of $A$ agrees with its exact inverse to a relative
error of about $2\times10^{-12}$.

## Application: Continuous Least-Squares Approximation

### Theory

The continuous least-squares approximation to a function $f(x)$ on $[0,1]$ using
the basis $\{\phi_0, \phi_1, \ldots, \phi_{n-1}\} = \{1, x, x^2, \ldots, x^{n-1}\}$
minimises $\int_0^1 \bigl[f(x) - p(x)\bigr]^2\,dx$ where
$p(x) = c_1 + c_2 x + \cdots + c_n x^{n-1}$.

Taking partial derivatives leads to the **normal equations**

$$
G\,\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{y},
\quad
G_{ij} = \langle \phi_{i-1},\phi_{j-1}\rangle = \int_0^1 x^{i+j-2}\,dx,
\quad
y_i = \langle f,\phi_{i-1}\rangle = \int_0^1 f(x)\,x^{i-1}\,dx.
\tag{9}
$$

Since $G_{ij} = 1/(i+j-1)$, the **Gram matrix $G$ is exactly the Hilbert matrix
$H_n$**.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Definition — Gram Matrix

The **Gram matrix** $G$ is the matrix of inner products:
$G_{ij} = \langle \phi_{i-1}, \phi_{j-1} \rangle$.

When the basis is $\{1, x, x^2, \ldots, x^{n-1}\}$ with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle = \int_0^1 f(x)g(x)\,dx$, the Gram matrix equals $H_n$.
:::

The coefficient vector is $\mathbf{c} = H_n^{-1}\,\mathbf{y}$.  With the exact
formula (7)–(8) for $H_n^{-1}$ the inverse carries no rounding error and each $c_i$
comes out in closed form.  Because $H_n$ is ill-conditioned, $\mathbf{c}$ is
sensitive to errors in $\mathbf{y}$, so the $y_i$ must be known to many digits.

### Example 3 — Degree-4 Polynomial Approximation of $\cos x$ on $[0,1]$

Find the continuous least-squares polynomial of degree 4 that approximates
$f(x) = \cos x$ over $[0,1]$.

**Setup.**  The basis is $\{1, x, x^2, x^3, x^4\}$ so $n = 5$ and $G = H_5$.
The right-hand side vector has components

$$
y_i = \int_0^1 x^{i-1}\cos x\,dx.
$$

Evaluating by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= \int_0^1 \cos x\,dx = \sin(1) \approx 0.84147, \\[4pt]
y_2 &= \int_0^1 x\cos x\,dx = \bigl[\sin(1) + \cos(1) - 1\bigr] \approx 0.38177, \\[4pt]
y_3 &= \int_0^1 x^2\cos x\,dx = 2\cos(1) - \sin(1) \approx 0.23913, \\[4pt]
y_4 &= \int_0^1 x^3\cos x\,dx = 6 - 5\sin(1) - 3\cos(1) \approx 0.17174, \\[4pt]
y_5 &= \int_0^1 x^4\cos x\,dx = 13\sin(1) - 20\cos(1) \approx 0.13308.
\end{aligned}
$$

**Solution.**  The coefficients satisfy $H_5\,\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{y}$, so
$\mathbf{c} = H_5^{-1}\,\mathbf{y}$.  Computing the matrix–vector product with the exact integer matrix $H_5^{-1}$ (and using high-precision values of $y_i$) yields

$$
c_1 = 25\,y_1 - 300\,y_2 + 1050\,y_3 - 1400\,y_4 + 630\,y_5.
$$

Substituting the integral values:

$$
c_1 = 25\sin(1) - 300\bigl[\sin(1)+\cos(1)-1\bigr] + 1050\bigl[2\cos(1)-\sin(1)\bigr]
- 1400\bigl[6-5\sin(1)-3\cos(1)\bigr] + 630\bigl[13\sin(1)-20\cos(1)\bigr].
$$

After collecting terms the coefficient simplifies to
$c_1 = 13865\sin(1) - 6600\cos(1) - 8100 \approx 0.999986$, close to but not equal
to $\cos 0 = 1$: a least-squares fit need not pass through $f(0)$.

The same row products give all five coefficients:

$$
\begin{aligned}
c_1 &= 13865\sin(1) - 6600\cos(1) - 8100 \approx 0.999986, \\[4pt]
c_2 &= 156480 + 138360\cos(1) - 274800\sin(1) \approx 0.000415, \\[4pt]
c_3 &= 1227870\sin(1) - 641340\cos(1) - 686700 \approx -0.502729, \\[4pt]
c_4 &= 1048320 + 1018080\cos(1) - 1899520\sin(1) \approx 0.006496, \\[4pt]
c_5 &= 945630\sin(1) - 516600\cos(1) - 516600 \approx 0.036152.
\end{aligned}
$$

The terms of each row product are large (up to about $3\times10^4$ for $c_4$) and
cancel to leave small coefficients, so the $y_i$ must be accurate: with the
five-decimal values of $y_i$ shown above, the same exact $H_5^{-1}$ gives
$\mathbf{c} \approx (0.99665,\ 0.0612,\ -0.7581,\ 0.3836,\ -0.1449)$, in which
only $c_1$ is right even to two decimals.  With the $y_i$ in full double precision,
both the exact $H_5^{-1}$ and a floating-point solve of $H_5\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{y}$
give $\mathbf{c}$ to a norm-wise relative error of a few parts in $10^{12}$.  The resulting
degree-4 least-squares polynomial is

$$
p(x) \approx 0.999986 + 0.000415\,x - 0.502729\,x^2 + 0.006496\,x^3 + 0.036152\,x^4,
$$

as Mathews also finds.  Its coefficients are close to, but not the same as, the
Taylor coefficients $1, 0, -\tfrac{1}{2}, 0, \tfrac{1}{24}$ of
$\cos x = 1 - \tfrac{x^2}{2} + \tfrac{x^4}{24} - \cdots$, because least squares
spreads the error over all of $[0,1]$ instead of making it small near $x=0$.

**Verification.**  Substituting the exact $\mathbf{c}$ back gives
$H_5\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}$ identically.  Compare $p$ with $\cos x$ at
$x = 0$ and $x = 1$:

| $x$ | $\cos x$ | $p(x)$ | error |
|-----|----------|--------|-------|
| $0$ | $1.00000$ | $0.99999$ | $1.4\times10^{-5}$ |
| $1$ | $0.54030$ | $0.54032$ | $1.7\times10^{-5}$ |

The largest error on $[0,1]$ is $1.7\times10^{-5}$ (at $x=1$), against
$1.4\times10^{-3}$ for the Taylor polynomial $1 - \tfrac{x^2}{2} + \tfrac{x^4}{24}$.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Key observation

The Gram matrix for the monomial basis on $[0,1]$ *is* the Hilbert matrix, so the
normal equations inherit its ill-conditioning: with
$\kappa(H_5) \approx 4.77 \times 10^5$, errors in $\mathbf{y}$ can be magnified by
up to that factor in $\mathbf{c}$.  For $n = 5$ double precision still has digits
to spare, but the margin shrinks quickly as $n$ grows.  The exact $H_n^{-1}$ gives
the coefficients in exact closed form (integer combinations of $1$, $\sin 1$ and
$\cos 1$ here), so they can be evaluated to any precision.  It removes the error of
inverting $H_n$, not the sensitivity of $\mathbf{c}$ to errors in $\mathbf{y}$.
:::
